standard_prerequisites: the theory Q and its provability relation
the representation formalism A_f for a function f in Q
composition h = f after g of number-theoretic functions
core_obligations: Prove that if h(n) = f(g(n)) with f and g representable in Q, then h is representable in Q: for h(n) = m, Q proves A_h(num n, num m)
proof_roadmap: Write h(n)=m as f(g(n))=m and put k = g(n)
Since A_g represents g, Q proves A_g(num n, num k); since A_f represents f, Q proves A_f(num k, num m)
Conjoin the two theorems and existentially generalize on the intermediate value y, obtaining Q proves exists y (A_g(num n, y) and A_f(y, num m)), which is A_h(num n, num m)
difficulty_reason: A direct two-step derivation using only the definition of representability and basic Q deductions (conjunction introduction and existential generalization); short but must be tracked through the representation formalism, hence H2.
